As someone who loves map-based games like Civilization and EU4, card games have also had a special place for me from time to time. They combine this love beautifully and immerse the player into a generic world. It's definitely an experience worth trying.Thank you.
画风可爱，玩法经典的一款精致小巧的回合制肉鸽游戏，非常上头。
撑到第三个星球直接被干爆了，应该是星球的特性，护盾被打了剩余一点不能留到下一回合用，小费法术有了但是缺少关键克隆人连锁伤害，清不掉后面扎堆的小怪。每隔一段时间就有外星飞船来干我的飞船，还得腾出费用上盾，个人感觉难度跨越大，几次都是在第三个星球被干爆，不是被飞船打爆，就是满屏的小怪清不掉，压力拉满了。整体游戏评价不好玩，过两天再来看看给好评这群人玩这游戏有没有超过20小时。
扮演殖民资本家，称霸外太空！ 游戏的卡牌构筑框架很成熟，各种喜闻乐见的要素基本都有，可以把克隆人士兵突变成各种有趣的特殊形态，同时还能给他们上各种装备，以及你在地图上还能造各种建筑，很有意思。
第一个飞船感觉很有意思，有种rts的感觉，第二个相对来说就乏味很多，几乎是纯凑牌比胡的，没防没加血小人一碰就碎，还没加速，建议重做奥。除此以外，护盾和小人的系统也相对割裂，建议再多打磨打磨
很有创意，但这数值是人玩的？飞船血量上限40，对面直伤9点开始每回合上涨一点每两回合造成一次，（9+11+13+15=48）假设9回合结束游戏，敌人每回合只需要一费处理，每回合一费叠三甲两次是6甲，这样才能不受伤害，飞船的血量回复方式是商店一次回8点
肉鸽新赛道说是，在肉鸽基础上加上战旗的玩法，目前刚通关凡难度，能感觉出这游戏真的很有潜力啊，玩的变异流派，删牌还是你肉鸽底层逻辑，把基础小人和盾删干净了，用建筑塔每回合产紫色小人上变异，把费用压下去了，配合装备塔减一费武装队伍，拿下异变体轻轻松松，豪丸👍

制作组拿脚填的数值，你开盾，任务完不成，你做任务就等着掉血。现在就是拿血量换任务，虽然商店能回血，但杯水车薪，纯纯慢性死亡。最恶心的是你遗物还有限制，那你每个星球给一个遗物点数有什么用？哦，我打了几个星球去商店你告诉我，我只能装3个遗物。要是你说你遗物做的很强力就算了，遗物数值小气到感觉数值策划是两个人，一个我就喜欢大的，一个我多给一点我会死。而且你现在的解锁机制有什么意义，卡的数量少，对于整体游戏体验没有明显提升，新卡和旧卡形成不了明显体系，新卡与游戏事件也形成不了明显的正收益。 最脑瘫的是制作组搁那刷好评还刷上瘾了。
纯粹的两个系统，一个是固定的，没有任何方法能改变的——每两回合基地扣血（多拖几个回合就暴死，伤害数值一点都不平衡），必须单纯的加防护。一个是小人的行动，要清怪，要找资源，要完成任务。这两者只能说是毫无关联，基地只能被动挨打，哪怕地图上一个敌人都没有，小人就是满地图乱跑，也没任何提示，做任务动不动就是方向错了，要么sl，要么拖几回合扣大血。 总结：玩起来非常难受，没有爽点。
游戏挺有新意的，卡牌和经营相结合，肉鸽随机性也做得不错，还是有可圈可点之处。不过玩多了就理解这游戏的核心就是召人＋叠甲，这两个的强度决定能否通关。
卡牌玩法是常见的选分支路线行进，策略玩法也是常见的六边形地块派遣单位每回合行动，但是结合在一起就意外地给人一种惊喜感，流派目前粗略来看应该是装备流，突变体流和一个发明流，好像还有弃牌流之类的玩法，不过可能目前解锁的内容还不够，感觉比较少暂时还不能成型，总体而言还挺有意思的
诶嘿嘿，扮演资本家，称霸外太空，但是这个称霸过程可没有那么简单，越来越苛刻的数值，难度简直大大的。不过，天衍五十取其一，还是尚有一线天机，翻牌，胜利，并非木有可能，就看玩家自己的选择~

我很少给游戏打差评，除非忍不住。数值是用脚填的，叠甲就没法做任务，做任务就掉血；遗物限制三个就算了，数值给的也太保守了，8%不消耗行动值是人能填出来的数值啊？30%还差不多。还有你那个破翻译，只能说不如机翻，我切英文版用有道翻译才看明白你那卡牌描述什么意思，一共就那几张卡，你矫正一下很难吗？

游戏设计上更像一款结合了rouge元素的放置类桌游,游戏目标需要玩家操控小人移动或战斗去实现，通过对基地的定期袭击制造软性的回合数要求。配合可爱的画风和太空背景的滤镜，让我有很高的游玩欲望。 但深入了解后只能说目前还需要改进的地方有点多，游戏难度过于简单，前期初始卡组就能无损过渡，后期单抽卡配合加费随便无限，很快就让游玩方式固化了。移动速度的属性过于重要，更快的完成任务等于更少的护盾卡去应对袭击，生命作用的途径太少。建议制作组增加玩家获取卡牌的数值，增大前期战斗压力使玩家多拿牌，或者以洗牌加费的方式限制无限。

Clonizer, developed by Juicy Plume and published by Rogue Duck Interactive, is a refreshingly inventive blend of turn-based strategy, roguelike deckbuilding, and base-building mechanics, all wrapped in a quirky sci-fi aesthetic. It carves out its own niche within the crowded indie strategy genre by embracing a cheerful, cartoonish visual style and mixing lighthearted humor with genuinely thoughtful gameplay. At its core, Clonizer puts the player in command of a team of “Clonees,” bio-engineered beings deployed to colonize and conquer procedurally generated alien planets. Each mission challenges the player to navigate a hex-based world while managing resources, outsmarting enemy forces, and building up their territory using a card-driven system that evolves over the course of a run. The first thing that stands out in Clonizer is its playful presentation. The game avoids the grim tone typical of many sci-fi colonization titles and instead opts for a more whimsical, family-friendly approach. The Clonees are goofy and endearing, the environments are colorful and varied, and even the enemies carry a comedic flair that makes encounters amusing rather than intimidating. The UI is clean, intuitive, and functional, which allows players to focus on decision-making without being overwhelmed by complexity. Despite the light tone, the underlying mechanics are surprisingly rich. Players must explore planets tile by tile, capturing territory, harvesting resources, and carefully deploying Clonees to maximize efficiency. Every decision feels meaningful, and the consequences—positive or negative—often ripple through the rest of the mission. Central to Clonizer’s gameplay is its card-based system, which governs everything from combat actions to construction, upgrades, and special abilities. Cards are divided into several thematic “departments,” each with its own strategic flavor, encouraging players to experiment with different combinations to create synergistic builds. This system injects a satisfying layer of unpredictability and depth, as every new run offers different cards, upgrades, and blueprint opportunities. Over time, players unlock more departments and cards, expanding their strategic toolbox and increasing the game’s replay value. The deckbuilding mechanics are handled well, never overwhelming the player but always offering new ways to approach challenges. Clonizer walks the fine line between accessibility and depth, making it easy to pick up but difficult to master. The game’s procedural generation ensures that no two missions play out the same. Each planet features a unique layout, enemy placements, terrain modifiers, and random events that require players to stay adaptive. Exploration feels meaningful thanks to the strategic importance of tile control and the occasional unexpected encounter, like running into bizarre alien traders or uncovering mysterious anomalies. These dynamic elements help to keep the experience fresh, even after multiple runs. The roguelike structure also adds tension, as poor decisions or unlucky draws can quickly spiral into defeat. That said, the game avoids feeling punishing—players are encouraged to learn from failure and try new approaches with each run, especially as new departments and Clonee abilities are unlocked over time. While Clonizer excels in creativity and gameplay variety, it’s not without its flaws. The difficulty can feel inconsistent, especially in mid-to-late game missions where enemy strength spikes abruptly or the randomness of card draws can work against the player. Some card synergies feel less viable than others, and a few balance issues may lead to frustration if a player builds a strategy around mechanics that are underpowered. Additionally, while the humorous writing and quirky tone add charm, the narrative layer is thin. There’s little in the way of overarching story or character development, and most of the game’s progression is driven by mechanical goals rather than narrative ones. For players looking for a deep lore experience or emotional storytelling, Clonizer may feel a bit superficial. Despite these shortcomings, the overall package is impressive, especially considering the small size of the development team. Clonizer shows a clear attention to detail and a genuine enthusiasm for its own concept. The visuals are polished, the mechanics are engaging, and the user experience is smooth and satisfying. It's easy to appreciate how much love and creativity went into the project, and for its modest price, it delivers excellent value. The pacing is also a highlight—missions are contained enough to be played in short sessions, yet rich enough to demand strategic thinking and long-term planning. Players who enjoy short, repeatable challenges with evolving complexity will find Clonizer’s structure rewarding. In the end, Clonizer stands out as a smart, funny, and surprisingly deep strategy game that rewards experimentation and creative thinking. It’s an ideal pick for players who enjoy deckbuilding mechanics, turn-based tactics, and the procedural unpredictability of roguelikes. Though it may not cater to those who prefer tight narratives or meticulously balanced competitive play, it offers more than enough originality and gameplay variety to carve out a place among the best of recent indie strategy titles. For fans of games like Slay the Spire, Into the Breach, or For The King—especially those who appreciate a bit of humor in their strategy—Clonizer is a refreshing and worthwhile addition to the genre. Rating: 8/10

中文翻译稍微有些问题，目前看来基本都集中在后勤部门里，比如移动飞船的蛮多牌都错翻成移动克隆人了，还有像艾利戈护盾干脆就不知天地为何物了……明明是“抽一张牌然后把所有电涌牌都移到最右”，不知道为什么能翻译成“下次打出时，获得少1点的护盾”。 不过游戏本身素质很强，既有rts造建筑爆兵的味道，又有战棋桌游的感觉，而底子又是很经典的爬塔式卡牌肉鸽，这三者融合起来非常和谐，玩起来别有一番风味，是足够创新的卡牌肉鸽形式。而过关的方式也有创意，不同星球地图搭配不同任务，比如有采矿的，有坚持存活九回合的，还有让克隆人跳进传送门紫砂的，不同的任务要求使得大部分奇奇怪怪的牌都能一定用武之地，并不是只有打怪才能过关，这也让游戏的风味能在传统的打打杀杀上更进一步，算是近期体感最优的肉鸽卡牌了。

This is a pretty neutral review really, but I'm going to put it on the recommend side because I enjoyed it for a while and I can see there being a place for it, for the right kind of person or the right kind of time. For me it's not really that, because the very slow unlock progress and general lack of variety makes it a bit of a slog to play. If you were stuck only being able to afford one game for a month, like a kid in the eighties, then this would be a great pick because you easily *could* play it for a month and still be somewhat enjoying it. But in the modern landscape of having more games than you have time to play, I don't want to sink a month into a game that I'm only *somewhat* enjoying, when I could be playing 6 other games to completion instead, and fully enjoying them. A single run also takes a long time, and generally everything feels a bit slow - not the UI and animations, which are fine, but rather that most of the time your units can each only move one space per turn. On planets with heatwaves, where you have to move to a safe tile every few turns or die, this can be super annoying because you want to go 'west' but you have to spend an entire turn going 'east' because the safe tile to the west is two turns away, then another whole turn to get back to where you were, so it's three entire turns to take a single step in the direction you're trying to go. Only three-ish (may be more if you have zero-cost cards or energy boosting cards, but is often less because you can also have two-cost or three-cost cards) card-actions per turn also makes it feel like things are going slow. And then for the final battle you have to deal 50 damage to the boss, where most things do one or two damage, so again it tends to be a long slow slog. And then you win, and it unlocks like 1.5 levels of stuff, which is 2 new cards, that doesn't really change anything. There's different starter decks which are another different slog to unlock, and it seems they differ by two minor cards from the basic starter deck. There seems to be only two "main classes" which, to be fair, have a reasonable amount of difference between them, but only two. It's possible escalating the difficulty would be more interesting, I haven't tried, but I find it hard to imagine, given how everything else is, that the higher difficulty isn't just "exactly the same but everything hostile has 50% more health". If it *is* more interesting then the game should more strongly recommend it when you win, whereas it feels to me like mostly the game is recommending *not* turning up the difficulty. So yeah, this sounds like a pretty negative review overall, but I'm leaving the thumbs-up because there's nothing really *wrong* with it, it's just not as fun as a whole mess of other tactical deckbuilders, such as Alina of the Arena, Fights in Tight Spaces, and StarVaders. About comparable to Roguebook, which has most of the same flaws described here.
